question: What are some ways to overcome the heating issue due to residual optical absorption in the integrated optomechanical devices?

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies redesigning the device from a traditional 1D nanobeam to a quasi-2D optomechanical crystal cavity as a primary strategy to reduce optically induced parasitic heating.
examples: Moving from 1D nanobeam OMCs to quasi-2D cavities lowers the hot bath occupancy
A 2D cavity design substantially reduces heating compared to the 1D nanobeam geometry
Dimensional expansion of the OMC from 1D to 2D mitigates residual optical-absorption heating

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: Answer explains the mechanism: the 2D geometry provides a larger surrounding area and greatly enhanced thermal conductance to the cold reservoir of the surrounding chip, consistent with ballistic phonon transport models and FEM simulations.
examples: FEM simulations with ballistic phonon transport predict a thermal conductance ratio of ~42 between 2D and 1D cavities
Thermal conductance to the surrounding chip is increased by 68x compared to 1D devices
The 2D design has more surrounding material to conduct heat away

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: Answer describes the dual role of the 2D phononic bandgap structure: shielding/protecting the acoustic cavity mode while phonon modes above the bandgap serve as extra channels carrying heat away from the cavity region.
examples: Phonon modes above the acoustic bandgap act as additional heat-removal channels
The phononic bandgap shields the breathing mode while higher-bandgap modes carry heat away
The 2D bandgap material both isolates the mechanical mode and provides heat-dissipation channels

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies slab-on-substrate optomechanical crystals (e.g., with bound states in the continuum) as a route to dissipate heat through the substrate.
examples: A slab-on-substrate device architecture allows heat to flow into the substrate
2D slab-on-substrate OMCs with mechanical BICs provide radiation channels for heat dissipation
Placing the crystal on a substrate lets heat phonons radiate into the substrate

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: Answer proposes short-pulsed optical excitation so heating occurs only during the pulse on-time while the resonator cools during the off-time, with phonon generation controlled by pulse duration.
examples: Pulsed pump limits optical heating to the on-time of the pulse
During the off-time, optical heating is negligible and phonon occupancy decays exponentially
Tuning pulse duration controls the number of heat phonons generated

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: Answer notes when substrate-based dissipation helps: at low temperatures (<1 K), where material absorption is also suppressed, or when substrate and slab thermal conductivities are comparable, since oxide conductivity at room temperature is ~100x lower than silicon.
examples: Oxide substrate conductivity is two orders below silicon, masking the benefit at room temperature
Substrate benefit becomes evident below 1 K, relevant for GHz-mode quantum experiments
Material-absorption loss is suppressed at low temperatures

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: Answer provides quantitative support, e.g., the factor-7.2 reduction in hot bath occupancy for the quasi-2D cavity and the power-law scaling of hot bath occupancy with intracavity photon number.
examples: Hot bath occupancy magnitude dropped by a factor of 7.2 for the quasi-2D cavity
Hot bath occupancy follows a power law in intracavity photon number, same as 1D nanobeams

ingredients.name: valuable_2
ingredients.criterion: Answer connects reduced heating to outcomes such as achieving effective quantum cooperativity Ceff > 1 under continuous-wave pumping, or enabling phonon sensing and quantum experiments with GHz mechanical modes.
examples: Reduced heating allows Ceff > 1 under CW optical pumping
These architectures enable phonon sensing and macroscopic quantum oscillator experiments
